original_question: Prove that the positive imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are not all rational multiples of one another.
target_in_paper: Theoretical problems, #1, Problem 2: "Prove that the positive ordinates of ζ(s) are not all rational multiples of one another."
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s official formulation. It has the correct function (the Riemann zeta function), the correct zeros (nontrivial zeros), the correct restriction to positive imaginary parts (the paper calls these positive ordinates), and the correct objective: to rule out the possibility that all such ordinates are rational multiples of one another.
missing_details: The paper explicitly uses the term "ordinate" and defines an ordinate of an L-function to be the positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero.
To be fully stand-alone, the question should define a nontrivial zero of ζ(s) as a zero ρ with 0 < Re(ρ) < 1.
It should explicitly say that only positive ordinates are being considered, not both signs of the imaginary parts.
The phrase "not all rational multiples of one another" should be made unambiguous, for example by stating that there is no single real number t > 0 such that every positive ordinate γ belongs to tℚ.
The problem is posed unconditionally; RH, GRH, SZ, and LI appear only as surrounding notation/motivation, not as assumptions of the problem.

The next item in the paper gives the narrower special case "show that γ1 is irrational," so the refined version should remain at the broader Problem 2 level and not collapse to that concrete instance.
refined_question: Let A := {Im(ρ) : ζ(ρ) = 0, 0 < Re(ρ) < 1, and Im(ρ) > 0}, the set of positive ordinates of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Prove that there does not exist a real number t > 0 such that A ⊆ tℚ.
justification: This paper is a problem list, not a theorem/proposition paper, so the nearest official formulation is Theoretical problems, #1, Problem 2 on page 2. Your draft matches that statement essentially verbatim. The nearby context needed to make it fully stand-alone comes from the Introduction, which identifies the distribution of zeros of L-functions and the linear independence of their imaginary parts as a central topic of the list (p. 1); from the Notation section, which records the LI notation and the meaning of γ1 (pp. 1–2); and from the opening sentence of Theoretical problems #1, which defines an ordinate as a positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero and explains the LI motivation (p. 2). The immediately following Theoretical problems #2 on page 2, "Show that γ1 is irrational," is presented only as a concrete instance of the broader problem, so the correct target is #1, Problem 2 rather than the narrower γ1 question.
